title: "Good to be Here"

> “It is good to be here.”

With those simple words, the 18th President of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints began his address at a BYU Devotional.

Having served as the President of Brigham Young University from 1971 to 1980, he could have said, "It is good to be back."

The public welcomed him with the warmth reserved for a beloved leader returning to his home.

His message was a call to action: an admonition for those tasked with fulfilling the prophetic destiny of the **Lord's University** to draw closer to the Savior.[^1]

[^1]: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bv-AQGCrKNI

It was a fitting homecoming for a man whose life started and expanded in and around Provo, Utah.

As I watched this public return, I found myself reflecting on the nature of homecomings that usually don't happen in public.

![](images/20260127_084832.jpg)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

My father was a part of famous brigade in the Korean army, the 3rd Infantry Division[^2] also known as the 백골부대(白骨部隊)

[^2]: <https://namu.wiki/w/%EC%A0%9C3%EB%B3%B4%EB%B3%91%EC%82%AC%EB%8B%A8>

The infantry beginnings are noted as,[^3]

[^3]: https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EC%A0%9C3%EB%B3%B4%EB%B3%91%EC%82%AC%EB%8B%A8\_(%EB%8C%80%ED%95%9C%EB%AF%BC%EA%B5%AD)

> Young men from the **Northwest Youth League** who had fled to the South after suffering under the brutal actions of the **Communist Party** volunteered to enlist in the military. They became the core members.., and they would fight the Communists and defend their country.

I learned about this, by talking with his youngest brother recently. My uncle had assumed we all knew this fact.

In keeping with the stoicism of his generation, my father avoided the association, believing that honor is not claimed but revealed.

He lived with a quiet independence, content to wait for the history to catch up and confirm what he already knew to be true.

He had endured private struggles and had overcome. He didn't need or want a public reminder of the battles of the war.

![](images/20260207_134122~3.jpg)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

> "A prophet is not without honour, but in his own country, and among his own kin, and in his own house" (Mark 6:4, KJV)

Fortunate are those who have loved ones waiting--those who remember exactly who you are--and demonstrate,

> “...while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion for him; he ran to his son, threw his arms around him and kissed him."

-   Luke 15:20 NIV

But even for those without personal connection or earthly recollection, the desire remains.

It is a universal desire to return home, whether that home is a physical address, an emotional state, or a spiritual origin.

Perhaps, then, the passage in Mark can be viewed through a different lens of hope.

As we grow, as we serve, and as we eventually turn our attention toward a home, the mindset shifts.

The scripture might be modified to reflect our shared human journey:

> A person is received with honor—and with love—in his own country, and among his own kin, and in his own house.

Until that day...
